🚀 Team ADECCE – Galactic Ace

We are three middle-school students and our teacher mentor from Özel Antalya Yükseliş Koleji, Antalya, Türkiye, working on the Space Mission Design Game challenge.

Galactic Ace is a 3D Unity game: players design their own spacecraft within a budget and a mass limit, then fly missions to 22 Solar System destinations (planets, dwarf planets and moons) and learn real space science along the way.
summary: Galactic Ace is a 3D educational game for middle-school students that turns the Space Mission Design challenge into a playable journey through the Solar System. Before every stage, players design their own spacecraft under two hard limits: a budget (in million dollars) and a launch mass (in kilograms). They choose a launch vehicle, a power source (solar panels, RTG or batteries), protection (heat shield, radiation vault, Whipple shield, parachute), an engine (chemical or ion), an antenna and up to three science instruments. A design report then shows how these choices shape the mission: solar panels far from the Sun or no heat shield at Venus make the mission harder. Players unlock 22 destinations (8 planets, 5 dwarf planets, 9 moons), each with four stages of rising difficulty and one of seven mission types inspired by real missions such as Juno, Cassini, New Horizons and Europa Clipper. Questions based on NASA Science content, quizzes and Codex cards turn every mission into learning. The game runs offline on Windows.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Galactic Ace is a 3D learning game for students aged about 10 to 14. It answers the Space Mission Design challenge by letting players design, manage and fly their own missions across the Solar System. Every stage starts with mission design and ends with a playable simulation that shows the result of the player's engineering choices.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Design: Before each stage the player builds a spacecraft within a budget (million $) and a launch mass limit (kg). Options include light, medium or heavy launch vehicles; solar panels, large solar panels, an RTG or a battery pack; a heat shield, radiation vault, Whipple shield, parachute and pressure hull; chemical or ion engines; low- or high-gain antennas; and up to three science instruments. Better systems cost more and weigh more, so every choice is a trade-off.

2. Report: A design report explains strengths and risks, for example that solar power is weak near Neptune, that Venus needs a heat shield, or that Jupiter's radiation needs protection.

3. Fly: The player then plays a mini-game whose difficulty depends on the design. There are seven mission types: heat control (Mercury, Venus), hazard flying (Earth, Jupiter, Saturn), landing (Mars, Moon, Titan), antenna aiming (Uranus), flyby photography (Neptune, Pluto), orbit insertion (Ceres, Ganymede) and ice drilling (Europa).

4. Learn: When players get stuck, Mission Control asks a question about that world; a correct answer gives help or a bonus. Each world ends with a final test, a quiz and a Codex card.

5. Progress: There are 22 destinations in three themes (8 planets, 5 dwarf planets, 9 moons), each with four stages (25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) of rising difficulty. Finishing a world unlocks the next one. Coins buy astronaut suits and spacecraft paints. The grand finale unlocks free exploration of the whole Solar System, then a return to Earth with atmospheric entry, parachutes and an ocean splashdown, followed by a learning summary and a certificate.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission trade-offs are usually abstract for students. Galactic Ace makes them visible and playable: students see that a design decision changes what the mission can do. It connects real planetary science to action, builds curiosity through choice, and fits both classrooms (short missions that fit into a lesson) and independent play. It runs offline on Windows with no installation, so schools with limited internet can use it.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

Unity 6 (Universal Render Pipeline) and C#. The user interface is built in code. Spacecraft models come from NASA 3D Resources, planet and moon textures from Stellarium, and facts and questions from NASA Science. Mouse, touch screen and keyboard are supported.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Instead of one long simulation, every world has its own mini-game based on what real missions had to do there. Help is given as a science question, so learning is part of the game loop. We kept missions short, the language simple, and the game playable offline. Mission ideas were inspired by real missions such as MESSENGER, Magellan, Mars 2020, Juno, Cassini-Huygens, Voyager 2, Dawn, New Horizons, Europa Clipper, ESA JUICE and JAXA MMX.

USE OF AI

Claude (Anthropic) assisted with writing and debugging C# code, with writing and translating in-game text and presentation text, and with preparing the slide decks. Some presentation background images were generated with AI tools in Canva and are labelled "Background: AI-generated image" on the slides. No AI-generated content uses NASA logos or branding. The team designed the game idea and scenario, chose the worlds and missions, shaped the learning journey and tested the game.
